name: Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs
tile_uses: The weekend braise, the farro bowls, the one-pot chicken
why_now: There's nothing seasonal about chicken. What changes in November is the weather: the first cool evenings make an hour-long braise appealing again, and bone-in, skin-on thighs are the cut built for it. This is the month's cut.
how_to_choose: Skin that covers the whole thigh, not shrunken back
Pink, plump meat with no gray edges
No liquid pooling in the package
Similar-sized thighs, so they cook evenly
buy_this_much: 6, about 2½–3 lbs: the braise, with four left for the farro bowls. Four more if you make the one-pot chicken with white beans.
price_note: Bone-in, skin-on thighs are one of the cheapest cuts in the case, well below boneless.

flavor_paths.name: Braised
flavor_paths.description: Seared, then an hour in the oven with leeks, fennel, and satsuma.

flavor_paths.name: One pot
flavor_paths.description: Seared in the Dutch oven, then finished over white beans and chard.

flavor_paths.name: Pulled
flavor_paths.description: Leftovers off the bone, into soup or onto toast.

weekday_uses: Leftover braise, pulled off the bone over farro
In the Dutch oven over white beans and chard
weekend_use: Seared and braised in the Dutch oven with leeks, fennel, and satsuma. The weekend dish.
storage: In the coldest part of the fridge, in the package, for a day or two. Cook within two days of buying.
one_thing_to_learn: Thighs are done at 165°F but better at 175–195°F: dark meat has connective tissue that keeps softening as it cooks, so a braised thigh at 195°F is more tender than one pulled at 165°F, not less.
market_question: Do you have them skin-on, bone-in?
